Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Consequently, this research highlights the significance of considering triangle-based interactions and hidden geometry in condensed matter physics, and provides a versatile model suitable for applying to other complex networks. Although specifically examined in the context of nanoassemblies, the model can be adapted to other scenarios, such as brain networks during seizures or social connections during conflicts. In these cases, the model may reveal similar phenomena, like the emergence of critical states or noise generated by the network's intricate geometry, that could have far-reaching implications for understanding and controlling these complex systems.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Furthermore, we observed a decline in energy flux with increasing distance from the solar surface, but with a key feature being that it became less intense lower down, which we believe is influenced by solar wind instabilities that accelerate electrons and influence the distribution of protons, although more research is needed to fully understand this behavior. Lastly, we analyzed the contributions to the decline in energy flux and found that the decrease in electron temperature plays the biggest role, followed by the decline in electron speed, then protons speeds, and finally the decline in electron density, although the impact of the last one is minimal. The main conclusions of our study are relevant to ongoing research about the solar wind's generation, as well as its influence on the solar interior, and we suggest more investigation is necessary to fully comprehend the behavior of solar wind energy near the solar surface. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly suitable for large-scale simulations required by modern cosmic microwave background experiments. The tool is openly available at https://github.com/ricardogens/s4cmb. The current version of's4cmb' focuses exclusively on experiments using bolometric detectors, but the package's architecture makes it easy to expand to other detector technologies in the future. The package includes an interactive command-line interface as well as Python API options for user customization. The package includes examples of both interface and API usage available in its documentation. The's4cmb' tool has already been utilized in actual research, with references to such studies listed in its documentation. The package can simulate a single detector's signal or a full array of detectors across the experiment, and it is capable of saving the simulated data in various compatible formats. The package also offers various graphical visualization options for the simulated signal and associated spectral and temporal instrumental systematic effects. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. Our research emphasizes the significance of incorporating linguistic representations inherent to pre-trained language models when they are applied in various NLP tasks. The code and data used in this study are available at the following link: https://github.com/salemtang/word_ordering.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our system's versatility allows easy integration into popular deepfake detection datasets and platforms, enabling straightforward deployment in real-world settings. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Additionally, we explore specific cases for degrees $n=6,7,8$ and note that for $n=4,5$ all inequalities are proven or conjectured to be equivalent to a standard form. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound involving the first main coefficient of a curve's Jacobian and the largest minimum, thereby generalizing and improving existing results. Lastly, we investigate the relationship between successive minima and the number of points on a curve, including an unsolved conjecture of Bombieri, and provide a survey of related results and conjectures in the literature.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our data coverage spans from the launch of the scheme in April 2020 until the end of October 2021, a period during which the scheme distributed approximately $321 million to users. Our study sheds light on the intricate operations of a peer-to-peer pyramid scheme, the financial costs incurred by users, the limited geographical spread of the scheme, the deceptive tactics used by its promoters, and the significant plaudits received by its creator, with implications for the regulatory environment of the blockchain industry. Our research also utilizes transparent code and transaction data available to the public, an unusual occurrence in research about Forsage. Nonetheless, due to the limited nature of available data, our study cannot pinpoint the individual identities of users or those involved in promoting the scheme, which prevents it from taking a more individualized approach in its analysis. Nonetheless, our research demonstrates that a community-driven investigation is feasible about a peer-to-peer pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, an unprecedented occurrence that highlights the contradictory nature of the scheme's publicity and operations. Our research is available online at the domain www.forsage.io/analysis, where it includes the code used to simulate transactions, videos promoted by Forsage, as well as interactive graphs about the scheme and its users. Our study conveys a significant lesson for users about the necessity of examining the code of a smart contract carefully before using it, as well as for the importance of being cautious with videos and social media content promoted by unknown individuals. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have published the research in the form of a catalog featuring the basic properties of the 19 candidates evaluated in this study. We have also included 19 additional previously documented bulge cluster candidates based upon RR Lyrae star research, combining the two lists to create a comprehensive catalog of 38 candidate globular clusters within the galaxy's bulge. We have analyzed the distribution of these candidates on a map of the galaxy's bulge and discovered a concentrated group of clusters located near the galaxy's central region and another more scattered group found further away from the center. We have also discovered a particular group of clusters moving at a faster rate through space and located at a greater distance from the galaxy's center. We have further investigated the metal composition of these candidates over time and discovered a negative correlation between increasing metal composition and older ages. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This indicates that even mild ribbons in longer wavelengths can contain extreme far-ultraviolet radiative signatures in both stellar and solar flares. This research is an extension of the earlier results presented in paper I, which focused on the 1992 June 9 AD Leo flare, and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the two-component electron beam model and its relation to ribbons and kernels in both stellar and solar flares. This knowledge can be applied to exoplanetary environments and opens up a new area of investigation for TESS, Kepler, K2, and future space missions that observe in the near-ultraviolet. This involves developing a bio-UV indicator that takes into account the level of ribbons and kernels on a planet's surface and their distance from the star, which affects the UV environment and thus the development of life on that planet. This research was conducted using data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, available through the IRIS IDB, and the Kepler space telescope

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. This work shows that taking into account influence and the underlying dynamics of systems can result in more reliable and scalable community detection, and highlights potential applications in open, dynamic systems. This research is showcased through an interactive dashboard available at: http://www.youtrack.cr.ffset.com. This work is also presented at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, we discover that the sparse coding component can be adapted for post-hoc representation learning on existing pre-trained models, leading to further performance gains. The code for SparseGAN is available at this link https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. Specifically, the open star cluster Cascadia offers promising findings, with a discovery rate for microbial life forms potentially high as 100 percent in this cluster, although further research is needed to confirm these results. Although the hypothesis of interstellar panspermia is plausible, it's essential to note that it's just one of many possible explanations for the discovery of life in certain stellar environments. A more advanced model is also proposed that takes into account factors like how microbial life forms can be affected by different stars and the distribution of scattered planetary material, all to better understand the mechanisms underlying the detection of life in the context of interstellar panspermia.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our research delivers capture-recapture models that can be used by itself to analyze resource selection, and new models that integrate capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate population density, space usage, and resource selection simultaneously.  We apply and evaluate these methods with real data to demonstrate their functionality.  We also provide R code to facilitate implementation. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles of our testing theory are under development and we welcome feedback and suggestions from anyone with an interest in this topic. The geometric testing theory has been applied to a real-world project, an open-source email program, to demonstrate its capabilities and the effectiveness of this approach. The code for this program, along with the testing framework and tools, is available for public use under the Apache Open Source License. The website www.geometric-testing.org provides more information about this project. The experiences and lessons learned from developing this project have been presented at a conference, an overview of which can be found in a separate paper also available online. The website includes source code, testing reports, and graphical error representations that illustrate the testing process and the geometric structure of the program being tested. The development of geometric testing started as a side project of the NICTA Verification Infrastructure Laboratory, located in Sydney, Australia. The initial funding for this project came from the Australian Government Department of Communications and the Arts. The development of geometric testing also received support from the Australian Research Council. Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. This action results in the set's equivalence to the set defined by the root system $\Phi_0$. This action also yields the system $\Phi_0$ as $\Phi$ in the scenario where $\Phi$ is of type $D_4$. The action on the set, however, is not free as it contains the invariant element $e_\delta$ and the action is not transitive as it is not possible to transform $e_\alpha$ into $e_\beta$ if the angle between the roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is less than $\pi/3$. This action is also not simple as it contains the invariant subgroup defined by the subset consisting of the roots and their multiples of $2$ times $\delta$. This action is free, transitive, and simple in the scenario where $\Phi$ is of type $A_l$, with the number of elements being $(l+1)(l+2)/2$. This action is also equivalent to the action described in the paper titled "Orbits of vectors in some representations. I". The paper also discusses the action's invariance under the diagram automorphism defined by the twist of the root $\delta$ with a shift of $2$ times $\delta$. This action on the set results in the set's equivalence to the set consisting of elements of the form $e_{\alpha+2\delta}$. This action is free, transitive, and simple in the scenario where $\Phi$ is of type $A_l$, with the number of elements being $(l+1)(l+2)/2$. The paper also examines the action's application to the specific root system defined by the figure shown in figure 1, which is of type $A_4$. The paper also derives the number of elements in this scenario, which is $15$.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm is proven through a probabilistic argument of large numbers, specifically the law of large numbers applied to small, independent, and identically distributed random variables. Our achievement is characterized by executing a simple protocol across the network that consists of random message transmission attempts between nodes, as well as calculating the frequency of successful transmissions, which serves as the basis for the size estimation. The accuracy of the algorithm's size estimation is validated through the analysis of its underlying protocol, specifically by examining the properties of the graph constructed from the transmission history, which is proven to be approximately equivalent to the original network. The algorithm has an insignificant additional node cost of O(log^2(n)), not including the cost associated with the node executing the algorithm. Our results also include two reference networks with different node distributions - the random regular graph and the Barabasi-Albert model - in order to demonstrate that the algorithm's performance is unaffected by the uncertainty of the network structure. Our achievement is further highlighted by comparing our results with an alternative estimation method based on centralized network knowledge, which is possible under the same conditions of uncertainty, as well as with a different model of uncertainty where the malicious nodes have limited processing power. Our results show that this alternative method is significantly more precise but requires a much larger node cost of O(n), which is in contrast to the depth-sensitive node cost of the proposed algorithm. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
The method's effectiveness is also demonstrated by incorporating the estimated
queue lengths into a simple decision-making protocol for optimizing signal
timing, which leads to reduced queue lengths and traffic speeds similar to the
baseline. The study includes free downloadable data from probe vehicles used in
the analysis. The proposed methodology is suitable for low-cost, real-time
implementation on traffic management platforms. The approach can also be
applicable to other scenarios involving short-term estimation of various traffic
states. The method's simplicity makes it compatible with combinatorial optimization
algorithms, offering a promising direction for future research. The data set is
available at no charge for use by other researchers and industry practitioners. 
The method can be utilized for static traffic state estimation as well. The study
also presents a new approach for estimating the probability of queue length, which
can be realized by probe vehicles that fail to detect queues due to premature
clearing. The proposed method's ability to incorporate failure-to-detect queues
due to premature clearing is innovative. The approach uses a Negative Hypergeometric
distribution to model these estimates, which is verified by analyzing real-world

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. A specialized public code has been developed to showcase and expand upon this technique, offering users an easy-to-adapt framework for solving hamiltonian constraints numerically. This code can be downloaded from [1,2]. Despite the method's current limitations to static spacetime configurations, we anticipate that its principles will inform future developments, potentially leading to an enhanced understanding of numerical relativity with dynamical matter sources.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We find that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a small value of approximately 1.1$\times 10^{-5}$ cm$^2$/K, and our results also highlight the potential of this material to exhibit very little drift in measurement, likely due to its unique magnetic properties and thin film configuration, thereby influencing the experimental accessible range. Our study highlights the potential of Mn$_3$NiN films in thermal to electric field conversion applications, and the straightforward experimental setup used could be adapted for other low magnetization materials. We also propose a simple drift free measurement protocol suitable for this class of materials. Our data and analytical modeling indicate a small temperature dependence of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and Nernst voltage, and we attribute this to a combination of nematic electronic domain wall motions and ferromagnetic impurities. Our findings further demonstrate the fundamental connection between the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects, and the unique magnetic properties of Mn$_3$Ni N resulting from its complex electronic structure, which could be useful for understanding and manipulating the anomalous Nernst effect in this material. We conclude by assessing the potential of this material in a thermal to electric field conversion device, and explore ways in which the anomalous Nernst effect could be enhanced through proper film growth conditions. Our approach provides a framework for investigating the anomalous Nernst effect in other low magnetization materials. Our data has been made publicly available through the Solid State Sciences Multidata Repository.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. We demonstrate this approach across scattering and spectroscopic measurements at the COHEREN, HiTES, and IDD beamlines at the NSLS-II. All code used in this study is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/NSLS-II/ML-at-NSLS-II. We invite users and developers to collaborate and contribute to this framework, embracing open standards and methodologies to ensure interoperability and ease of maintenance. By open-sourcing this work, we aim to accelerate the development of high-quality machine learning models for real-time analysis across user facilities, promote reproducibility, and facilitate educational opportunities for scientists. To this end, we provide an interactive version of the paper available at https://ml-at-nsls-II.github.io/. All data generated during this study can be found in the data repository at https://doi.org/10.17188/1336520. All code and data mentioned in this study are licensed under the terms of the MIT License. We warmly welcome users, beamline scientists, and machine learning experts to the NSLS-II machine learning community. We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given the growth restrictions imposed on the function $f$, with respect to the gradient variable, we find that when the obstacle function is bounded and satisfies certain regularity conditions, the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ being part of the Sobolev space, leads to a corresponding increase in the differentiability of the solution, provided the partial map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a $W^{1, p+2}$. Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$. Additionally, when considering the associated parabolic problem, we obtain enhanced regularity properties for the solution, where the differentiability index increases to three, i.e., from $C^{1+\alpha}\left(0<T;\mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right)$ to $C^{2+\alpha}\left(0<T;\mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right)$. In both cases, we establish the latter property for $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^2$ and $a\in W^{1, p+2}$. Lastly, we provide specific examples that demonstrate our results' applicability to a broad class of problems.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles. Ultimately, this leads to a calculation of certain explicit weights related to finite fields. The method also yields a concise proof of local, infinite field case specificity, where w_2(S_k^p) equals w_2(S_k) for a given field k. The approach extends pally to GL_2 through the means of Weil representation, with the inclusion of non-abelian extensions handled via classification of certain G_K-Artin-Scheier sequences. This in turn leads to a calculation of weights related to a specific family of Hilbert modular forms over Q(\sqrt{5}) and another family over Q(\sqrt{14)). The approach can be further extended to GL_2 through the use of p-adic Hodge theory, with the resulting combination allowing for the calculation of weights related to certain infinite families of Hilbert modular forms. The paper is accompanied by an appendix co-authored with M. Diamond and F. Tonini. The relevant proofs are adapted from the original sources, with the results presented in a simplified and sometimes different form. The paper is aimed at an audience consisting of graduate students and researchers with an interest in number theory. The related publications can be found at arXiv:2103.04544 and arXiv:2103.04545. The paper has been previously published in issue 32 of the Journal of European Mathematical Society, with the copyright belonging to EMS. The paper was originally submitted on the 12th of February 2020. The results presented in the paper were previously mentioned in the talk titled "From p-adic Hodge Theory to Serre's Conjecture for GL_2" delivered by the author at the conference titled "Automorphic forms and related topics", which took place in Kyoto, Japan, from the 3rd to the 7th of March 2014. The results were also mentioned in the talk titled "Kummer theory and the weight part of Serre's Conjecture for GL_2"

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of projects that utilize composite materials, from aerospace to sports equipment. 
Furthermore, by utilizing conductivity rather than surface projections, it offers a level of accuracy that other detection methods cannot match. 
The novel approach can also be modified to utilize other imaging and analysis techniques, as well as cell-based methods, by replacing the specific physical model of conductivity with general detection signals. 
In its current form, the technique has potential applications in fields beyond composite materials, including medicine and astrophysics, anywhere that involves complex configuration reconstruction based on partial and indirect measurements. 
The proposed algorithm has been thoroughly tested and proven to be robust, even with limited amounts of data, and has the potential to be scaled up to more intricate configurations and larger scales, as evidenced by the successful reconstruction of impact-induced delaminations. 
The integration of EIT and genetic algorithms delivers a level of accuracy in reconstructing damage dimensions that other detection methods cannot match, making it the best available option for keeping composite materials in their optimal condition. 
The proposed method offers a novel way to determine the required spacing between carbon nanofiller layers, as well as the type of layering, in composite materials, and can be used to validate existing formulas and models that predict the distribution of fillers and conductivity in composite materials, and to refine them to deliver a level of accuracy never before

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This discovery was previously reported in arXiv:2005.01242 and arXiv:2008.04428, and it serves as a significant expansion upon the results presented in arXiv:1811.00544 and arXiv:1911.00168. Additionally, it yields precise expressions for the descendant fields derived via the Miura transformation in arXiv:2106.05372 and arXiv:2106.05373. This approach also facilitates the derivation of explicit expressions for the descendant fields in the Liouville conformal field theory following from the presence of higher-spin symmetry. These expressions were previously unidentified within the mathematics literature, and they serve as a significant expansion upon the results presented in arXiv:2106.05372 and arXiv:2106.05373. Furthermore, it enables the identification of degenerate fields and the determination of four-point correlation functions whose boundary values satisfy hypergeometric differential equations of any arbitrary order. This yields a comprehensive expansion upon the results presented in arXiv:1811.00544 and arXiv:1911.00168. This was previously reported in arXiv:2005.01242 and arXiv:2008.04428. Moreover, it facilitates the classification of hypergeometric differential equations

This consequence is shown to hold true for a broad class of buildings, inclusive of certain types of graph structures known as apartment systems. These findings build upon previous research by Bestvina and Kapranov, who established that the right-angled Coxeter groups with which these buildings are associated are biautomatic. The study also reveals that biautomatic sequences can be determined for these groups using natural geometric methods. The results obtained in this study are applicable to a wide range of buildings, encompassing certain types of graph structures known as apartment systems, and allow for the characterization of uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings as those with specific biautomatic properties. The research further involves developing an alternative proof of a previously established theorem by Swarztman, according to which the free product of two biautomatic groups is itself biautomatic. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of ECoG-based BCIs in the direct control of advanced walking prosthetics, offering a significant improvement over previously reported EEG-based alternatives. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Lastly, our model's flexibility enables seamless integration into existing workflows, offering a suitable substitute for static models without requiring substantial workflow modifications. We publicly release DECENNT's code and an accompanying demonstration website to facilitate further research and practical adoption.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for fields such as biology, zoology, and environmental science, where the ability to automatically identify biolocomotion from video footage could provide valuable insights and facilitate easy access to relevant data. A detection framework for biolocomotion is envisioned for the future, capable of revealing the species behind the observed movement with the help of additional sensors and knowledge. The code and datasets mentioned in this paper are available at https://github.com/amirpapazian/Biolocomotion Detection.

Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. A brief comparison is also drawn with results from a related, yet distinct, binary on/off power control analysis. A possible path for future adaptation on systems that reach the extremal gain of $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ is also proposed, suggesting that in these situations, a transition from binary power control to optimal power control could be facilitated by implementing a variety of simple, or 'elementary' operations on the network. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm provides greater flexibility in simulating flow dynamics with a wide range of particles, allowing for a much larger range of Reynolds numbers. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, this system's performance was tested under sudden ground changes and showed its capability to recover quickly. Lastly, to enhance efficiency and reduce energy consumption, a optimal control strategy based on the Poincaré section method was implemented, which resulted in the robot reaching the desired height in three hops instead of five. This research provides a comprehensive approach to controlling a one-legged hopping robot on soft ground, which can be applied to higher-dimensional legged robots. Also, this project's findings are relevant to other hopping robots, whether biologically based or not, and offers a platform for further development, including the use of more sophisticated terrain simulation and optimal control algorithms. Lastly, a discussion on the implications of this research for legged robot locomotion on soft ground is presented. This project was made possible by the grant number NNX15AQ58A from NASA. The simulation software used in this research is available at www.cfdlab.com. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/amin-vahreza/Force-Control-on-Spherical-Granular-Material. The simulation of this research was conducted on the high-performance computing cluster, named Tethys, which is maintained by the University of Texas at San Antonio. The code for this project is compatible with MATLAB and can be downloaded at https://github.com/amin-vahre

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM generates hierarchies by identifying latent topics that correspond to specific network nodes, thereby ensuring the resulting models align with the original network structure. Moreover, we demonstrate HDTM's capability to handle massive datasets by analyzing Wikipedia's complete content, comprising over 6 million articles and 13 million links. The resulting model, with 720 documented hierarchies, serves as an example of HDTM's scalability in action. The HDTM code is available open-source on GitHub, allowing for easy adaptation and incorporation into existing applications. The model's capabilities are further illustrated through an interactive visualization of the Wikipedia hierarchy available on our website. The HDTM framework offers a scalable and suitable method for generating hierarchies from complex information networks, especially for web-based applications, and our results show that the model excels at capturing the underlying network structure, even in extremely large datasets. The proposed method provides a concise summary of each node's contents, making it ideal for searching within the network, and the resulting topic models remain accessible for in-depth analysis. The scalability of HDTM also facilitates exploratory data analysis, as evidenced by our examination of Wikipedia's content, where we discovered distinct themes related to geography, company names, and abstract concepts like time and energy. The model's ability to generate coherent topics during the analysis of Wikipedia further underscores its effectiveness. The proposed algorithm serves as a foundation for future enhancements, as our results demonstrate that the current implementation already yields high-quality results, and the code is optimized for ease of use. The documentation for the code, available on GitHub, includes a detailed guide to installing the required dependencies and a tutorial on using the HDTM model, including an example analysis of Wikipedia. The results from our experiments are also presented in the documentation, which is accessible at our website. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the artificially generated nature of these simulations, the results hold significant value as they provide a concrete, quantifiable example of the quench-annealing duality, offering a qualitative or, in more extreme cases, a 10-fold speedup in solution-finding compared to standard quantum annealing algorithms. Nonetheless, further investigation is necessary to extend these results to more realistic, non-artificial settings. The current study builds upon prior research that demonstrated the relationship between the quench dynamics and the quantum annealing gap along with its impact on the solution-finding efficiency in quantum annealing. Prior research utilized a single quench trajectory for the purpose of obtaining the minimal annealing gap, which, as noted earlier, is challenging due to the artificial nature of simulated Hamiltonians. In contrast, the current study employs an ensemble of quench trajectories, which, as shown in the simulations, results in an accurate reproduction of the annealing gap's functional behavior. As such, the artificial nature of simulated Hamiltonians no longer poses an issue. The proposed approach can be applied to real-world scenarios of the exact cover problem by first conducting a preliminary quantum annealing trial to obtain the initial quench trajectory, which in turn enables the reproduction of the annealing gap's functional behavior. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon.

coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band

which arises solely from this single model.

between weight transfer, screening, and the extra pairs of energy levels, and
how sensitive the physics is to these factors, thereby cautioning against
over-simplification when modeling this class of materials.

energy levels as stable features is necessary to accurately capture the
physics, which in turn ensures valid predictions about the material's properties.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This may have implications for correcting zero points in parallax measurements derived from missions like Gaia. Finally, we discussed possible sources of $\gamma$ variation, including conventions used in converting angular units and the impact of this variation on the absolute magnitude zero point. Given these considerations, we recommend using a more precise unit conversion to minimize confusion and potential errors, also taking into account the observed variation in parallaxes on the ecliptic plane's axis, which may help constrain possible variations in $\gamma$ or other parameters affecting parallax measurements. This may have further implications for absolute magnitude zero point calculations, which we discussed in a broader context. Lastly, we highlighted possible multi-parameter implications, which we believe merit further investigation, also examining the impact on stellar mass estimates derived from Gaia measurements. This could involve re-analyzing simulation data and evaluating expressions relating mass and density zero point variations, along with determining usable precision limits for units and denominators in formulae used in astrophysical applications. This may also provide further insights into Gaia's accuracy and variable parameters affecting its measurements, which could be relevant to similar missions like PLATO. This could be achieved by investigating variables affecting density zero points and their possible effects on mass estimates, which we found to be minimal for the Gaia simulation.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The knowledge retrieved as part of this approach is also visualized to gain insight into the underlying semantics. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Careful.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials. The underlying code is publicly available at 
https://github.com/materialsmachinelearning/AluminumGNNDISORDER.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. Specifically, we examine the challenge of estimating the mean of a mixture distribution where the mixing distribution is unknown and the parameters of the mixture components are treated as constants, and we explore how GMLE's performance compares to the method of moments estimation method. Additionally, we investigate the efficacy of our GMLE approach in estimating the expected value of a function of the parameters of a distribution in sampling experiments using normal mixtures. Finally, we discuss how GMLE's can be applied to the problem of estimating the mean of a mixture distribution where the mixing distribution is unknown and the parameters of the mixture components can be recovered using an EM algorithm. This is achieved by using the fact that in the limiting case where the number of observations is infinite, the GMLE's are identical to the maximum likelihood estimation of the mixing distribution, which can be recovered using the EM algorithm. This reduces the estimation of the mixing distribution to the level of individual observations, rather than treating the parameters of the mixture components as constants, and provides a path for applying our GMLE's to sampling problems where the parameters of the mixture components cannot be treated as constants. This approach is then examined in detail using a normal mixture model. This includes recovering the GMLE's, investigating the properties of these estimators, simulating their performance in sampling experiments, and providing an analytical solution to the problem of estimating the mean of a normal mixture model.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% WER reduction on the NuSeD dataset. We also presented the results of our experiments on the Estonian dataset, which showed promising outcomes. Our code has been made available at this link https://github.com/certroroll/tedennavasr.
