Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/sentence-metadata-network.

In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. Finally, through our investigation, we also established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, the corresponding allocations are fair up to one good with respect to their underlying values. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Although a two-fold gap in the lattice data sets is observed when considering whether the quark and the corresponding antiquark are separated by one site or two, further investigation is needed to draw conclusions about the physical significance of this distinction. Additionally, questions arise regarding the influence of the quark's mass and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark are essential components of the pion's properties. Moreover, discrepancies with the predictions of chiral perturbation theory emerge, particularly in regards to the magnitude of the two-fold gap in the lattice data sets. As such, a more in-depth analysis of these phenomena through larger lattice data sets and more precise simulations is warranted. Our lattice results are made available through the figshare platform. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/SIT.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we established a record for the lowest possible score in TextWorld, a benchmark that takes around a week to complete on a single high-performance computer. 
TextWorldExpress is open to the public for downloading and can be used to create new optimized text-based games as well as enhance existing ones. 
Our findings have significant implications for conducting demanding tests with text-based games, providing a viable solution for solving the speed limitation problem. 
In addition, TextWorldExpress offers a suitable platform for researchers whose focus is on areas such as virtual agent safety, without a data size constraint. 
To facilitate smooth integration with existing games, we developed a flexible text-based game framework called TextWorldZero, showcasing the possible integration of TextWorldZero with classic games like TextAdventure and TextWorld. 
Our research also involves a style-guided refactoring of Python code, primarily taking up a significant portion of processing time, as well as an examination of the impact of different optimization strategies on performance. 
Finally, TextWorldExpress includes a feature for generating detailed analysis reports on the internal workings of text-based games, providing valuable insights that can be used to identify performance-bottlenecks. 
Our research was previously known by the name TextWorldOpt, but has been renamed to TextWorldExpress.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. This study provides a freely accessible toolkit for the cognitive science community, consisting of RStudio, Jupyter Notebooks, and PyMC3, that allows researchers to easily replicate our research and Bayes factor validation framework for their own studies. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experimental evaluations have validated the accuracy of DiscSense, and the findings are expected to contribute to the development of rigorous standards for the classification of English discourse indicators. Furthermore, DiscSense is available at https://github.com/THUQH/DiscSense.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, our research reveals gradient descent's ability to yield a sequence converging to a geodesically convex neighborhood, which justifies its practical success in many applications. Our main findings can be interpreted in the standard Burer-Monteiro context, serving as an explanation for the effectiveness of gradient descent in that setting. Our work assumes no particular distribution of the underlying data, making it a non-probabilistic analysis. Lastly, our results imply the existence of a geodesically convex neighborhood containing any stationary point, which can be an escape path for gradient descent, allowing it to leave areas with saddle points or areas that are not convex. Our research provides a new perspective on the Burer-Monteiro factorization, a comparison with other related factorization methods, and a strategy for choosing the factorization size. Moreover, our results lead to a discussion on the underlying geometry, the use of an alternative Riemannian quotient geometry, the fixed-rank positive semidefinite cone's geometry, and the presence of an excess variance term in the Burer-Monteiro factorization. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our pre-trained models and data are available for download at: \url{https://github.com/ghrua/MCSEC}.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Full investigation includes measurements
of several hadron ratios that indicate particle production consistency across Xe-Xe 
and Pb-Pb collisions based on midrapidity particle count, not overall multiplicity. 
Detailed analysis for centraleity bins, in addition to averaged values over all 
collisions, is presented to better capture energy dependence trends. Experimental
data for several centraleity bins also provide initial evidence of how particle 
ratios evolve with increasing energy. Conclusive research findings are based on
around 70 $\mu$b worth of Xe-Xe collision data, followed by analysis of 3.5 pb
worth of data. Dedicated ALICE collaboration research was used to obtain these
results.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. By extending the model to account for both dissemination and diffusion of rioting, as well as incorporating migration trends derived from census data, a better-fitting model was created to predict both the timing and frequency of riots in Santiago. Furthermore, this model highlighted the significance of population displacement in facilitating the emergence of epidemic hotspots, consistent with mathematical analysis. A financial cost was also incorporated into the model, which revealed that reducing disparities could delay the riots' decline, whereas increasing inequality might actually stimulate further unrest in the short term. A novel feature of this model, not present in its original form, is the way it calculates the core epidemic region through the minimum of a fixed constant or a critical value based on population density. This model's effectiveness in predicting riots in Santiago makes it a promising tool for analyzing other instances of social disturbance. The model's underlying principles also encourage further exploration of academic theories in sociology and biology that may underpin the riots, such as the concept of "altruistic fatalities." The model consists of a system of three non-local differential equations incorporating a response delay, which was solved numerically to simulate the disorders' temporal progression. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also explore ways to handle inequalities involving the complement operator and provide a step-by-step solution procedure. Furthermore, we investigate the application of our method to regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets, establishing a connection between the complexity of containment problems and the level of suffix alignment among involved regular expression components. We have implemented our algorithm in a proof-of-concept prototype called DeepRE and have conducted experiments to evaluate its performance on realistic datasets. Experimental results suggest that containment problems involving restricted contexts, such as finite sets of characters, can be efficiently solved using DeepRE, and the algorithm also demonstrates effectiveness in determining containment among regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets, offering a meaningful comparison with established baseline methods. We have released DeepRE as an open-source tool available for public use. This research has further implications for the containment problem involving regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets, providing a theoretical framework that can be applied to various underlying models, and offering a novel perspective on the problem complexity, captured through the alignment of suffixes among involved regular expression components. We have initially introduced this framework in a prior, shorter paper titled "Solving Regular Expression Containment with Infinitely Vast Character Sets" presented at the 21st International Conference on Fun with Algorithms, now expanded into this current research.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed method's superiority is also proven by evaluating the model on datasets with both smooth and sudden movement. The code is available at https://github.com/Shoukai-Liu/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Both theoretical and experimental findings can be generalized to higher-order semimetals, suggesting that 3D solid-state systems enriched with diverse nonlinear Weyl semimetal properties await discovery.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. A comparative analysis is also presented, where our approach is compared against the iterative and least squares regularized methods. The study highlights the method's potential advantages in terms of computational efficiency, particularly in high degree of heterogeneity scenarios. The reconstruction of missing boundary data for the Stokes and Navier-Stokes equations is also modeled and numerical examples provided. The study concludes with the method's extension to time-dependent problems and suggestions for further improvement. The research is complemented by public access numerical codes. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The resulting code is now available online, awaiting the contribution of model owners who can help further develop the FedSA framework. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This study highlights the potential of combined microwave and terahertz near-field imaging for assessing and improving the performance of quantum devices.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is tailored to contribute to the ongoing discussion within the scientific community and to guide future research and potential missions to study the planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere, as well as its complex interactions that have shaped and continue to shape Venus's evolution. This work is also part of the EXPLORERs team's efforts to study the environment and surface of Venus, as well as its interior and atmosphere, and to explore the planet's potential for habitability in the past, present, and future. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. One example data set, consisting of Twitter posts about two different topics, has been analyzed to illustrate the methods presented. One particular interesting finding from this analysis is the discovery of a topic that has a self-reinforcing relationship with itself, as well as the identification of certain words that contribute to these relationships. The methods introduced here can also be applied to other point process models, such as the nonlinear self-exciting integer-valued autoregressive model. The results we have obtained can be found on the arXiv website. The corresponding R package, called jnhawkes, is available on CRAN. The data set used in this study is available upon request. The nonparametric Bayesian estimation of the nonlinear Hawkes process has been previously unreported. The concentration rates of the posterior distribution have the potential to contribute to the theoretical foundation of various learning algorithms, such as Bayesian estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and contrastive divergence, which are commonly used in various applications, including neuroscience, finance, and sociology. The accuracy of the Bayesian estimator can be gauged through the mean squared error, which provides a measure of the distance between the estimator and the true value. The development of the nonparametric Bayesian estimation of the nonlinear Hawkes process has implications for the concentration rates of the posterior distribution, which can be extended to other models, such as random fields and random graphs, as well as Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning. The method introduced here can be compared to other methods of estimating the Granger connectivity graph, such as the maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian information criterion, and network sensitivity analysis, which are commonly used in various applications, including neuroscience

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. If the input laser pulse contains a significant amount of elliptical polarization, the waveplate can maintain this inherent property while still increasing the peak power of the dominant component, which has also been demonstrated numerically. This indicates that the plasma waveplate is a highly versatile component that can be applied in a wide range of situations, as shown in a simulation where it successfully enhanced the peak power of a laser pulse delivered to the focus of a beam transport system. This achievement highlights the capability of plasma waveplates to efficiently convert linearly polarized laser energy into more suitable circularly polarized energy, which is optimal for achieving high-field plasma interactions with a narrow angle of a laser beam, as well as the advancement of plasma optics components that can withstand and effectively utilize high-power laser pulse capabilities. The expected outcomes for optimal $CP$ observables in $\tau$-pair production at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV with $\tau^\pm$ decaying into leptonic or semihadronic modes are calculated, accounting for full kinematic information. For the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator, with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$ and assuming acceptance cuts, the achievable sensitivities for $d_\tau$ are estimated to be $6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm for semihadronic decays, respectively. In the ideal case without particle cuts, the achievable sensitivities with $50$ ab$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV, corresponding to $4.5 \times 10^{10}$ $\tau^+ \tau^-$ events, would be $5.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $3.2 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm, respectively. Additionally, the magnitude of the $\tau$ EDM form factor in the type-II two-Higgs doublet and scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model is investigated. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In contrast, a random error matrix can be corrected with a high probability of success of up to n-k code rates. Our main result also includes a constructive approach to create rank metric codes with the ability to correct symmetric errors of up to n-k rank. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams. This resulting expression can be compared to the original integral representation of the spinning block operator. The obtained geodesic Witten diagram representation can be related to the original integral representation of the spinning block operator through the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method, which allows us to determine the specific coefficients associated with this relation. The resulting relation between the geodesic Witten diagram and the integral representation of the spinning block operator is specifically analyzed in the context of conserved current conformal block operators. The derived relation between the geodesic Witten diagram and the integral representation of the spinning block operator takes the form of an explicit integral expression that can be evaluated to obtain the coefficients associated with this relation. The obtained two-point geodesic Witten diagram coefficients for the conserved current conformal block operator in CFT$_2$ are found to be directly equivalent to the coefficients obtained using the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method from the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator representation. The evaluation of the two-point geodesic Witten diagram coefficients for the conserved current conformal block operator in CFT$_2$ provides a non-trivial cross-check of the accuracy of the obtained relations, as these coefficients can also be determined using alternative methods. The obtained results suggest that the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation is a valid equivalent to the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator representation for conserved current conformal block operators in CFT

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo exploded with a high energy explosion mechanism, followed by a prolonged radiative era, resulting in a lengthy nebular phase. Thus, we observe SN~2020jfo as an extreme example of the already rare SNe~II with extended plateau phases. The presence of nickel in its nebular-phase spectra and the large hydrogen envelope in its progenitor are thought to be the result of its intermediate mass, which is also uncommon for Type II supernovae. The combination of these characteristics supports SN~2020jfo's inclusion in the rare class of Type II supernovae with short plateau durations. The absence of a massive helium layer in SN~2020jfo's progenitor is further evidenced by the presence of [Fe~II] line spectra during the nebular phase, as well as the low metallicity of its absorbed light during the plateau phase. The expansion velocity of SN~2020jfo's plateau phase was remarkably low, around 50 to 60 km/s, and the analysis of its [Ca~II] line spectra during the nebular phase revealed an all-Type II supernova velocity pattern. The comparison with other low-luminosity SNe~II, such as SN~1970G and SN~1994H, highlights SN~2020jfo's longer nebular phase duration

This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE concept can also be applied to other types of optics, such as micro-channel plate (MCP) X-ray optics. The MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments is sufficient for detecting a signal with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 at any sky direction within 10 days, and this duration can be significantly decreased by increasing the number of segments. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. 

These models have been compared to established theories and numerical solutions, with results showing they yield identical results when conditions are analogous, yet offering greater flexibility in modeling scenarios. This new methodology provides a more versatile tool for researching complex, rotating stellar evolution and has been implemented into the MESA code under the name'mesa::physics::relativity::rotating::lagrangian'. 

This method has a significant advantage in reducing computational errors associated with finite timesteps and grid resolutions, as it generates highly precise results with relatively coarse mappings. This approach has further been applied to simulate the collapse of rotating stellar cores, and has revealed unique characteristics in its results. 

Finally, this methodology has been discovered to converge with a unique order of 1.5 for both time-stepping and spatial resolutions, serving as a key area for future research. This approach offers a powerful and versatile tool for researching rotating stellar evolution and has been made available online along with its code and documentation.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We discuss the integration of this network with current detection algorithms used by electromagnetic observatories, which observe the full sky with a range of telescopes via the Transient Name Server. The developed code is publicly accessible via GitHub, presenting a foundational element for future deep learning investigations. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential for deep learning to excel at detecting the diverse range of merging compact binaries, and serves as a crucial step towards successfully identifying neutron star and black hole binary mergers in real-time.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Moreover, this study highlights the significance of studying pure behavioral changes and their lasting effects on urban diversity, along with the financial implications for individuals and businesses. Lastly, this work provides a framework for assessing the long-term impact of reduced interaction due to the pandemic, which can be applied to other contexts beyond urban diversity, such as the impact on tourism or cultural events. Finally, by analyzing the declining willingness to explore new places in the long term, this research raises concerns about potential lasting effects on individual personality traits, in line with psychology theories. The underlying dataset and code for this research have been made publicly available on GitHub, at https://github.com/lijin-usc/pandemic-urban-diversity. The results of this research have also been shared at various conferences and workshops, including the ACM Conference on Computing and Networking, the International Conference on Data Mining, and the Los Angeles Chapter of the Association for Computing Machinery. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. In addition, we demonstrate the capacitiy of our framework to extract pivotal information from misleading news, coupled with an accompanying visualization. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/AhmedHamdy267/TextSummationForFakeNews.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As evidence of its broad applicability, we also successfully utilized DynaSOAr to accelerate popular open-source SMMO implementations of popular object-oriented applications, including LBM and FDTD.  Our research and efficient DynaSOAr framework provide a foundation for easily parallelizing a range of previously overlooked applications on SIMD devices, as well as a scalable and high-performance solution for managing large amounts of data across object-oriented frameworks.  In particular, we found that DynaSOAr's performance gains are particularly visible in applications with low object counts and large domain sizes, including simulations with complex, open environments. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. This theoretical model highlights the importance of proper magnetic alignment and orientation of the YSR states in comparison with experimental data. Moreover, it emphasizes the critical role of orbital decomposition in understanding YSR state behavior and analyzing local states along the d-axis, which cannot be achieved through other analysis methods. Lastly, this framework's applicability to complex magnetic structures is demonstrated and may be utilized to predict YSR state behavior in other systems.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our findings also highlight the necessity for accurate supercell sizing in order to obtain reliable results, as an under-sized supercell led to errors including anti-ferromagnetic ordering and N-O bonding.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This relationship enables accurate prediction of the transition between these regimes, completing our understanding of the stick-slip to stationary transition in dry liquid foams. The findings of our study are relevant to various situations involving fluid dynamics, including the flow of liquids within porous media, emulsions, and foams, as well as the operation of devices like bubble columns and froth flotation equipment. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The data and code used in this report are available for public use.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/look-ahead-attention.

Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. By studying the past of grid computing, we aim to provide a useful example for the field of artificial intelligence. Just like grid computing, artificial intelligence faces the challenge of moving beyond theoretical applications. Therefore, artifical intelligence researchers should learn from the successes and failures of the grid computing community and draw parallels with their own work. Ultimately, we are confident that a translational perspective will become increasingly essential for the development of artifical intelligence. A comparative analysis of the two cases reveals additional knowledge that can be used throughout the field of artifical intelligence. We also explore the challenges that grid computing overcame and the lessons it gained, which will be useful for the development of artifical intelligence. Furthermore, we examine the various forms that grid computing took and the impact it had, as well as the methods that researchers used to break down complex technologies into more manageable components, making them more easily implementable, and the ways in which they combined multiple technologies into single, integrated systems. The study of grid computing can be applied to other projects in the field of artifical intelligence by providing answers to frequently asked questions about translational computer science, such as what kinds of research are considered translational, how can we evaluate the effectiveness of translational research, and what are the ethical considerations of applying artifical intelligence. The knowledge gained from grid computing can also be used to address the common challenges it and artifical intelligence share, including the difficulty of evaluating complex systems, the need for multi-disciplinary collaboration, and the challenge of moving beyond theoretical applications. The case study of grid computing can be broken down into three primary components: its development, implementation, and impact. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. We have made comprehensive theoretical predictions available for potential use by experimental teams. We have previously characterized the J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter but have now investigated the phenomenon for the first time. We have also examined the connection between J/ψ invisible decays and lepton or meson decay modes, identifying potential signals for light sterile neutrinos or dark matter. These include novel modes of muon or tau lepton decay assisted by neutrinos or dark matter, as well as rare charmed meson decay assisted by dark matter. These findings suggest that experiments focusing on charmed quark physics, such as the Super Tau Charm Factory, with significant collision energy and detection capabilities for charmed mesons and muons, can effectively explore J/ψ decay into invisible matter and related rare decay modes involving light sterile neutrinos or dark matter. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This achievement ensures IShTAR can accurately replicate conditions necessary for understanding and preventing plasma degradation in helical devices powered by ICRF waves.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this way of framing the task allows researchers to easily incorporate additional constraints, such as constraints based on the morphology of objects, which can be incorporated into the model by using binary regression masks to guide the density masks. This paper presents extensive experimental evaluations, comparing the W-Shaped Network to other state-of-the-art Baseline models, which yield a 5.85% and 6.50% relative improvement in Dice scores when detecting kidney cells and breast cells respectively. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/zhkslc/W-Net.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Finally, a validation of our findings through GCNN-based classification on multiple datasets shows the practical effectiveness of this approach. By breaking down the components of GCNNs, this approach offers a practical method for feature extraction, providing a performance that is on par with more complex GCNN models. A deeper understanding of GCNNs, along with this accessible analysis tool, may also be applicable to other CNN-based models. All code and data for this project are available online at \url{https://github.com/ghrasoul/GCNN-intuition}.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Specifically, the results show a 13.44% and 17.91% boost in the estimation of axial and lateral phase values respectively: a 57.07% and 45.28% improvement in the estimation of axial and lateral wave numbers; and a 53.57% and 25.69% increase in the frequency domain ratios of axial and lateral displacements. The outcomes of this research demonstrate the potential of VSSA-SA elastography in enhancing the estimation of mechanical properties of tissues. The proposed technique provides higher lateral resolution, increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction, and better frequency domain ratios than the current state-of-the-art techniques. Notwithstanding its advantages, VSSA-SA elastography faces challenges in imaging depths where the synthetic aperture technique loses effectiveness. Consequently, this research introduces a number of necessary modifications to enhance the technique's effectiveness in deeper imaging ranges. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We achieve this result using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method, and our analysis focuses on a simplified case to showcase the underlying approach. Furthermore, we provide a worst-case storage-probing variant that utilizes a storage capacity of $k \cdot (1-1/t)\cdot d$ dimensions and $\log t$ bits to store the parameter $t$, and demonstrate its applicability to large values of $k$. From a worst-case perspective, we establish a lower bound on the storage capacity required for solving the $k$-means clustering problem in the dynamic setting, which can be applied to the storage-probing model as well. This achieves a trade-off between the storage capacity and the number of centers $k$ with a factor of $d$ dimensions in the exponent, making it a more intricate lower bound than previously known. Our algorithm for the standard model has an approximation guarantee of $O(\sqrt{d}\cdot \Delta^{1/3})$, and the storage-probing variant has an approximation guarantee of $O(\sqrt{d}\cdot \Delta^{1/2})$, and both can be achieved within a single pass through the data stream. Our approach also provides a new static algorithm with the same approximation guarantee for a restricted class of $k$-means instances in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Additionally, we discuss a variant of the algorithm that enables a shift in the parameter $k$ without incurring additional storage, and a method for solving the facility location problem in the dynamic setting. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by focusing on macro-actions, our model can be adapted for application in large-scale real-world scenarios, including in robotics. All the code used in this research is publicly available. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. A comprehensive comparison is made between EW distribution functions and EW photon distribution functions, with a particular emphasis on near-universal adjustments, in order to further advance this field of research. A plethora of publicly available W/Z PDF and photon PDF tables at various energy levels is provided to facilitate this research. A initial assessment is carried out to examine the scope of applying a (polarized) weak boson distribution function to a muon collider, and based on this analysis a proposal is made to equip future colliders with a weak boson detection system at energy levels above 25 TeV, with a particular focus on the optimization of forward-moving detector components. A comprehensive examination is conducted to investigate the influence of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions on leading order 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels, with a particular emphasis on identifying the subset of reactions that are significantly impacted by these functions, with a proposal to restrict the application of these functions to this subset of reactions in order to conserve computational resources. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that separating tasks with modular networks
can lead to a significant decrease in performance degradation and an increase in
the discovery of new tasks. We hope that our research opens up interesting
paths to explore, especially concerning the relationship between task sharing and
catastrophic interference, and the unique challenges posed by continuous action
and observation spaces. To facilitate this, we make our code available open
source. Lastly, we discuss our findings within the broader context of transfer
learning and learning to learn.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By combining these results, we derive several notable consequences and theorems, including their original proofs, using a combination of their original formulations and modern formulations using the Godel operator and Kripke's schema. This combination also enables the derivation of some more advanced and complicated results, such as their extensions to the second incompleteness theorem, along with some unusual formulations requiring only a weak form of the beta-schema. This study originally grew out of an exchange on the FOM list in 2006, where the connection between the Godel operator and the beta-schema was discussed, along with the relationship between Godel's first incompleteness theorem and Tarski's undefinability theorem. This development can be seen as a part of the broader project of integrating the main results from metamathematics into the mainbody of mathematical logic. This integration involves replacing the conventional formulation of Godel's first incompleteness theorem with a form using the beta-schema, and acknowledging the multiple pathways to obtaining the Godel operator, which has significant implications for various applications and theorems. This development is also related to the widespread misconception that the beta-schema is equivalent to the Godel operator, along with some corrections to the errors committed by famous logicians such as Hilbert, Bernays, and Turing. This study demonstrates that there are logic systems that possess the property of epsilon-calculus without being equivalent to the Godel operator, which provides a proof of a theorem proposed by Georg Hatcher in 1986. This development is also shown to enable a simpler proof of a result attributed to French in 1988, along with some other results and theorems, including some formulated using the Godel operator and others formulated using the beta-schema. This study demonstrates that there are logic systems that possess the property of having a suitable form of the beta-schema without being compatible with the Godel operator, which in turn enables the construction of systems that are capable of expressing certain statements that claim the system is incomplete, without being trivially incorrect, as seen in the result proposed by George Boolos in 1993.
