In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Our method's strong performance was also matched by the results of more complex models requiring significant computational resources. Our code is available at https://github.com/shimothy/CGAN.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The contribution of this current work extends that of a preceding study, from which it differs by incorporating novel approaches to invariant configuration specification. We also derive novel conditions for the preservation of quadratic surfaces in fractional-order systems. The article concludes with an exploration of the relationship between invariant surfaces and the number of system equilibria they contain, as well as an analysis of the relationship between invariant surfaces and the system's stability properties. The article's findings are demonstrated using a fractional-order Chua's system. We also offer a commentary on the related results of a preceding study, from which the current work differs by considering the system's stability properties, rather than relying on the guassian property of an matrix. The article's content is accessible to a broad audience interested in systems and dynamics. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Furthermore, calculations determine the distance to this screen as well as the extent and characteristics of the void, contributing to the mapping of the Local Bubble's structure. Additionally, the analysis reveals a screen associated with a localized density gradient, boundary with the Leiden Cloud, and another linked to a prominent interstellar scintillation gradient, among other findings. The approach presented here for studying the screens and the surrounding interstellar medium can be applied to other pulsars, yielding comprehensive knowledge of the local astrophysical environment. The related data has been made publicly available. The discovery of a void associated with one screen provides insight into the structure of the Local Bubble, confirming earlier cloud boundaries and defining the boundary between the Local Bubble and the Leiden Cloud, specifically mapping the distribution of the Leiden Cloud and detailing the screen's dynamics and dynamics of the empty space. The analysis of density gradients of one screen also sheds light on the screen's dynamics and the surrounding interstellar medium. The approach presented here for studying the screens and the surrounding interstellar medium can be applied to other pulsars, yielding comprehensive knowledge of the local astrophysical environment. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Human evaluator ratings reveal that the proposed method exceeds the baseline WN model in terms of quality and pitch accuracy for unseen frequency inputs. Moreover, QPNet exceeds the state-of-the-art non-resolution-based baseline in speech reconstruction evaluation score (SRE), and surpasses WN in terms of SRE and naturalness scores for unseen frequency inputs. Code is available at: https://github.com/Parandkuhi/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, the theory of shadows is shown to be responsive to localizations of bicategories, thereby gaining the capability to compute traces via a process of localizing the bicategory in question. The theory of shadows is also found to be compatible with the process of shifting, which it achieves by shifting the bicategory. Moreover, the theory of shadows contains an intrinsic module structure, defined by means of composition in the bicategory of functors, which it utilizes to calculate traces via functors from the form N([C]). The theory of shadows is further demonstrated to be an enhancement of the theory of traces, thereby providing a general framework for defining traces on bicategories. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our source code is available for public use at https://github.com/zwang-leehose/localization.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/JinHePro/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and we treat it as a weak solution inverse problem, defining the stability estimate in the $L^2$ norm. This study also outlines numerical methods to solve this problem, including a gradient-type iterative algorithm and a conjugate gradient iterative method using a regularization approach. We demonstrate the uniqueness and stability of the solution using numerical experiments and offer a discussion on the reconstruction results using mesh size and time step size experiments. This research involves a model involving acoustic waves in a domain with a changing boundary, where we solve an inverse problem to determine the shape of the domain and the source term within the PDE model, and we outline a numerical strategy using a level set method to solve the problem. This study and its numerical aspects have been theoretically and numerically verified on a range of geometries from simple shapes to more complex shapes found in real-world applications. We also discuss a related problem of reconstructing an obstacle within the PDE model and outline a numerical strategy using a projection method and a level set method. This research contributes to the field of inverse problems and provides numerical solutions to inverse problems involving structural acoustic interactions. It also discusses the stability and uniqueness of the solution and the accuracy of the numerical methods used. This research paper is targeted towards an audience with an intermediate level knowledge of the subject matter, requiring background information on mathematical and numerical analysis, partial differential equations, and inverse problems and their numerical solutions. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This specific gauge choice can be achieved through a direct transformation of the standard harmonic gauge, using a suitable parameterization that ensures covariant properties are preserved.  This approach can be applied to both linearized and nonlinear gravity, although only the linear implementation is presented here.  The relationship between the harmonic gauge and Weyl's conformal flatness criterion is also worth noting.  The associated conformally flat metric can be determined through a complex integration, utilizing a complex harmonic gauge that extends basic harmonic gauge principles to complex geometry.  The resulting conformally flat metric exhibits desirable properties, including its ability to detect conformally flat metrics and its utility in solving the Einstein conformally coupled gravity in higher dimensional spacetimes.  The introduction of a mass term leads to a nonlinear massive gravity model based on the harmonic gauge, which can be analyzed using the standard perturbation theory, providing a linearized approximation and revealing the occurrence of tachyon behavior in some cases.  The proposal of a new variable that combines aspects of the harmonic gauge and direct metric comparison, allows for an alternative, simpler approach to analyzing the nonlinear massive gravity model. For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Moreover, a direct identification is obtained of the Metaplectic group elements that correspond to time-reversal symmetry within these dynamics. Lastly, the extensive application to the Harper model, a 1D discrete time-reversal invariant system, is demonstrated.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this approach may provide a richer learning experience compared to traditional approaches, incorporating both mathematical and graphical representations to demonstrate the validity of the formula for an average value, as well as the range of possible values for a given distribution. As such, this method can offer both instructional purposes and scientific insights for undergraduate students, researchers, and professionals in the field. As a supplementary example, we also examine the average energy of a Boltzmann distribution exempt from the zero-energy ground state scenario. As expected, this results in negative temperatures when the temperature exceeds a certain threshold, which in this case is equivalent to half the energy of the system's total. This can be visually represented in graphical form, offering an intuitive understanding of the concept of negative temperature. Moreover, this approach highlights the limitations of the Boltzmann distribution, highlighting the distribution's inability to account for situations where the energy falls below the ground state in comparison to the total energy of the system. As such, this report also examines the energy conditions necessary for the Boltzmann distribution to be considered valid. As a further illustration, we also examine the distribution of a two-level system following a quantum jump, resulting in a distribution that can be compared to the Boltzmann distribution. This comparison enables a deeper understanding of the relationship between temperature and population dynamics, as well as the conditions necessary for the Boltzmann distribution to be considered valid. As such, this report can provide both instructional purposes and scientific insights for undergraduate students, researchers, and professionals in the field. As a supplementary learning experience, we also provide Python code for calculating and plotting the Boltzmann distribution, available online. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we explore the intersection of all these conditions with those related to vacuum stability, neutrino characteristics, and the Higgs mass, across a range of top quark masses from 130 to 170 GeV. In doing so, we identify the necessary contributions of operator loops that maintain vacuum stability, as well as the required intensity for neutrinoless double beta decay experiments, given a desired sensitivity level of 10^-13. Additionally, we examine the interplay between the simplest scoto-seesaw and the Higgs near the critical temperature. Finally, we demonstrate that the simplest scoto-seesaw can be distinguished from other neutrino-seesaw frameworks based on dark matter phenomenology, specifically through the unique characteristic of solar dark matter, which emerges in the simplest scoto-seesaw model due to the inherent connection between the "solar" neutrino sector and the radiative solar sector. In this model, this aspect is made possible by the vast range of possible masses, extending below the electroweak scale, coupled with the fundamental dark parity symmetry that ensures that the lightest dark sector particle has a very small coupling with the standard model. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The generalization of our results to other geometries is discussed, along with the importance of precise $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ definition. The approach used here also allows for the relation of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing to other quantities, such as gradient correction, lattice constant ratio, or ratio of $d$-orbital to $p$-orbital occupation, offering a more comprehensive understanding of transition metal oxide magnetism. The associated raw data can be found at [https://github.com/AbhishekPandey/td_dos_mixing]. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our analysis and experiments demonstrated the capabilities of StyleGAN in medical imaging, paving the way for using GAN-based networks in healthcare. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application includes a user-friendly
graphical interface and is designed for novice and experienced users alike.
ViDaExpert is specifically tailored for object-feature tables and supports the
importation of tables from various sources. The application permits user-specified
modifications to algorithms and offers a vast library of 3D scene components
for creative 3D scene construction. Furthermore, ViDaExpert enables the
generation of customizable reports detailing computational processes and
analysis results. The application is platform-independent and available for
free download.
